To flitter means to move rapidly in a light, restless, back-and-forth or darting way — like something that can't quite stay still. Think of a candle flame in a breeze, or a butterfly that keeps zipping from flower to flower. That constant, quick, light movement — with no real settled destination — is the heart of what "flitter" means.

Sense 1: To flutter or flicker — moving rapidly back and forth

This is the most precise, dictionary-core sense. To flitter means to move back and forth very rapidly — the way a candle flitters. The movement is light and trembling, not heavy or forceful. A flame flitters. A leaf in the wind flitters. Wings flitter.

Sense 2: To move about quickly and nimbly from place to place

This is the broader, more common sense you'll encounter in everyday writing. To flitter means to move about rapidly and nimbly, or to move quickly from one condition or location to another. Here the emphasis is less on back-and-forth trembling and more on quick, light, restless movement across a space. Think of birds flittering back and forth between a backyard feeder and the safety of the trees.

Both senses share the same soul: light, quick, restless movement.

This is an important subtlety. "Flitter" is built from the word flit, but it carries something extra. It implies the action happening repeatedly, continuously — not just once. If something flitters, it isn't making one quick dart and stopping. It keeps going — back and forth, here and there, over and over. This is what gives the word its sense of restlessness and busyness.

When used literally, flitter describes the physical movement of real objects:

  • A butterfly flittering among flowers.
  • A bat flittering silently around a garden at dusk.
  • A flame flittering in the wind.
  • A flock of pigeons caused to flap and flitter around.
  • Monarch butterflies flittering and fluttering on a hike.

Notice the things that flitter are almost always small, light, and airborne — or at least delicate. Heavy things don't flitter. A truck doesn't flitter. A boulder doesn't flitter. The word carries an inherent sense of lightness.

"Flitter" is also beautifully used for things that aren't physical — ideas, feelings, time, particles. Anything that seems to dart about in a light, fleeting, hard-to-pin-down way can "flitter."

  • A writer's neuroses can flitter around him like fireflies.
  • Subatomic particles can flitter across the screen in a film.
  • A pocket of time can flitter away before you know it — gone almost as soon as it arrived.

In the figurative sense, "flitter" often carries a slight feeling of elusiveness — the thing is there, but it won't hold still, and you can't quite grasp it.
How It Compares to Similar Words

These words are all close cousins, and it helps to see how they differ:

Flit — a single, quick, light movement from one point to another. Sharp and sudden. One action. "The bird flitted to the branch."

Flitter — like flit, but repeated and continuous. The action keeps happening. "The bird flittered about the garden" — it kept darting here and there.

Flutter — more about the rapid, trembling movement in place or with wings/edges. A heart flutters (trembles). A flag flutters (waves rapidly). Flitter and flutter overlap a lot, and are often used interchangeably, but flutter tends to feel more about the trembling motion itself, while flitter tends to feel more about moving from place to place.

Flicker — mostly about light or something visual that rapidly shifts between visible and not — a flame flickers, a light flickers. Flitter can overlap with this too, but flicker is more specifically about the on-off quality of light or visibility.
The Overall Feel of the Word

"Flitter" is a word that feels exactly like what it describes — light, quick, and a little delicate. When you read or hear it, picture something small, airy, and in constant, restless motion — never settled, always moving, always just out of reach. Whether it's a butterfly above a meadow, a bat in the evening air, a thought darting through the mind, or a moment of time vanishing before you can catch it — that is what it means to flitter.
